q: What is a "Political Party"?
o: A committee of civil servants only
A group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government
An association of foreign traders
A wing of the judiciary
e: A political party is a group of people who agree on some policies and programmes for society and come together to contest elections and hold power.

q: What are the three main components of a political party?
o: The leaders, the active members, and the followers
Judges, police, and army
Farmers, traders, and banks
Governors, President, and media
e: A political party has three components: the leaders, the active members, and the followers.

q: Which of the following countries has a "One-party system"?
o: United States of America
United Kingdom
China
India
e: In China, only the Communist Party is allowed to rule, representing a one-party system.

q: Which type of party system exists in the United States of America (USA) and the United Kingdom (UK)?
o: One-party system
Two-party system
Partyless system
Military rule
e: USA and UK follow a two-party system where power usually changes between two main parties.

q: What type of party system does India follow?
o: One-party system
Two-party system
Multi-party system
Monarchy
e: India has a multi-party system where several parties compete for power and more than two parties have a reasonable chance of coming to power.

q: Which institution registers and recognises political parties in India?
o: Supreme Court of India
Election Commission of India
Ministry of Finance
NITI Aayog
e: Every party in India has to register with the Election Commission, which also lays down criteria for recognition as a State or National party.

q: In which year was the Indian National Congress (INC) founded, and what is its election symbol?
o: 1980, Lotus
1885, Hand
1984, Elephant
1925, Ears of Corn and Sickle
e: Founded in 1885, the Indian National Congress is one of the oldest parties in the world, with the Hand as its election symbol.

q: In which year was the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) founded?
e: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) was founded in 1980 by reviving the erstwhile Bharatiya Jana Sangh formed by Syama Prasad Mukherjee in 1951.

q: Under whose leadership was the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) formed in 1984?
o: Kanshi Ram
Jotiba Phule
Sitaram Yechury
Sharad Pawar
e: The Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) was formed in 1984 under the leadership of Kanshi Ram.

q: "Antyodaya" and "Integral Humanism" are core ideological concepts associated with which Indian political party?
o: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)
Communist Party of India (CPI)
Aam Aadmi Party (AAP)
National People’s Party (NPP)
e: The BJP draws inspiration from Deendayal Upadhyaya’s ideas of Integral Humanism and Antyodaya.

q: Which party was founded in 1964 and believes in Marxism-Leninism?
o: Communist Party of India - Marxist (CPI-M)
Nationalist Congress Party (NCP)
Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP)
Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)
e: Founded in 1964, CPI(M) believes in Marxism-Leninism and supports socialism, secularism, and democracy.

q: What does "Defection" mean in politics?
o: Putting up campaign posters
Changing party allegiance from the party on which a person got elected to a different party
Queuing at a polling station
Levying a new tax by the government
e: Defection means changing party allegiance from the party on which a legislator got elected to a different party.

q: Which party, formed in 2013 under the leadership of P.A. Sangma, became the first party from North East India to attain National Party status?
o: National People’s Party (NPP)
Trinamool Congress (TMC)
Aam Aadmi Party (AAP)
Biju Janata Dal (BJD)
e: National People’s Party (NPP), formed in 2013 under P.A. Sangma (symbol: Book), is the first political party from North East India to attain National Party status.

q: What is an "Affidavit" that every election candidate in India is required to file?
o: A party manifesto
A signed document submitted to an officer where a person makes a sworn statement regarding personal information, property, and pending criminal cases
Notice of the polling date
A bank loan certificate
e: Following a Supreme Court order, every candidate contesting elections must file an Affidavit giving sworn details of property and pending criminal cases.

q: When was the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) founded and what is its election symbol?
o: 2012, Broom
2005, Clock
1999, Lotus
2014, Hand
e: The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) was formed in 2012 following the 2011 anti-corruption movement; its election symbol is the Broom.

q: Which of the following is a core reason why democracy is considered better than other forms of government?
o: It promotes equality among citizens and enhances the dignity of the individual
It imposes instant decisions without any discussion
It does not require elections
It gives unlimited power to one dictator
e: Democracy is better because it promotes equality, enhances individual dignity, improves decision quality, resolves conflicts peacefully, and allows room to correct mistakes.

q: What is the most basic outcome expected from a democracy?
o: It produces a government that is accountable to citizens, responsive to their needs, and legitimate
It automatically becomes the wealthiest nation in the world
No citizen ever criticises the government
Parliament never meets
e: The most basic outcome of democracy is producing an accountable, responsive, and legitimate government.

q: What does "Transparency" mean in a democracy?
o: Citizens have the right and the means to examine the process of decision-making to verify if norms and procedures were followed
The government keeps all files secret
Election results are never announced
Only ministers may read laws
e: Transparency means that a citizen has the right and the means to examine the process of decision-making.

q: In which year was the Right to Information (RTI) Act implemented in India to promote transparency?
e: The Right to Information (RTI) Act, enacted in October 2005, empowers citizens to find out how government functions.

q: Why is a democratic government called a "legitimate government"?
o: Even if slow or less efficient, it is people’s own government chosen by citizens and enjoys overwhelming support worldwide
Because it comes to power without elections
Because it never collects taxes
Because it is ruled by a single dictator
e: A democratic government may be slow or less efficient, yet it is people’s own government and therefore enjoys legitimacy.

q: Comparing economic growth rates between 1950 and 2000, what does NCERT highlight about democracies vs dictatorships?
o: Dictatorships had a slightly higher rate of economic growth on average than democracies
Democracies grew 10 times faster
Dictatorships saw zero economic growth
Both recorded zero growth
e: Between 1950 and 2000, dictatorships recorded a slightly higher overall rate of economic growth, though the difference among poor countries was negligible.

q: Have democracies been fully successful in eliminating economic inequalities and poverty?
o: Yes, poverty has reached zero in all democracies
No, despite political equality, democracies do not appear to be very successful in reducing economic inequalities
Only monarchies reduce poverty
Poor people are barred from voting in democracies
e: While democracies rest on political equality, growing concentration of wealth among a few shows democracies have not been very successful in reducing economic inequalities.

q: Even though the poor constitute a large proportion of voters, why do democratically elected governments often appear less keen to address poverty thoroughly?
o: Because poor voters do not vote
Democracies have often failed to give adequate priority to poverty reduction despite the poor forming a large voting block
Because the Constitution forbids helping the poor
Because there are no poor voters left
e: NCERT notes that even where the poor make up a large share of voters, democratically elected governments do not appear as keen to address poverty as expected.

q: Which form of government is best suited to negotiate and accommodate social diversity peacefully?
o: Military dictatorship
Democracy
Absolute monarchy
One-party authoritarianism
e: Democracies usually develop procedures to conduct competition and peacefully negotiate social differences, whereas non-democratic regimes often ignore or suppress them.

q: What does the example of Belgium illustrate regarding social diversity in a democracy?
o: That a democracy can successfully negotiate differences among ethnic groups through power sharing and mutual respect
That the majority must suppress minority languages
That democracy fails in small nations
That only one language should be legalised
e: Belgium showed how democratic accommodation and power sharing successfully resolve differences among diverse linguistic communities.

q: In a democracy, what does "rule by majority" truly mean?
o: Permanent domination of the majority religious or linguistic community
Different persons and groups can and do form a majority in different decisions or elections, rather than permanent rule by a majority community
Banning minorities from voting
Overriding all court verdicts
e: Rule by majority does not mean rule by the majority community in religion, race, or language; it means different people and groups can form a majority in every decision and election.

q: Why does democracy stand much superior to any other form of government regarding the dignity and freedom of the individual?
o: Because passion for respect and freedom are the very moral and legal basis of democracy
Because democracies have no laws at all
Because only rulers enjoy freedom
Because criticism is forbidden
e: The passion for respect and freedom is the foundation of democracy, giving moral and legal force to struggles for equality by women and disadvantaged castes.

q: What is a distinctive feature of democracy that ensures its "examination never gets over"?
o: As democracy passes one test, it produces another test—citizens develop higher expectations and keep asking how to make it work better
A brand new Constitution is written every year
Students vote weekly
Elections happen only once in a century
e: As people experience some benefits of democracy, they ask for more; the fact that citizens complain and expect better reflects democratic awareness and success.

q: Which characteristic is typical of a non-democratic regime compared to a democracy?
o: Taking quick decisions without bothering about legislative deliberation or public opinion
Granting Right to Information to citizens
Allowing free criticism by opposition parties
Holding free and fair multi-party elections
e: Non-democratic rulers do not have to bother about deliberation in assemblies or majorities/public opinion, allowing quick decisions that may be unacceptable to people.

q: What is meant by "Political equality" on which all democracies are based?
o: Every citizen earning identical income
Every adult individual having equal weight in electing representatives (one-person-one-vote)
Every citizen joining the same party
Removing age limits for candidates
e: Political equality means all individuals have equal weight in electing representatives regardless of wealth, caste, religion, or gender.

q: Approximately how many political parties are registered with the Election Commission of India?
o: About 50
About 150
More than 750
Only 7
e: More than 750 parties are registered with the Election Commission of India, though not all are serious contenders in elections.

q: Which major function distinguishes political parties from pressure groups?
o: Organising public protests
Contesting elections, gaining political power, and forming and running governments
Publishing newspapers
Collecting charitable donations
e: Political parties contest elections directly and aim to form and run the government.

q: What vital role do political parties that lose in the elections play in a democracy?
o: They are permanently dissolved
They play the role of Opposition by voicing different views, criticising government failures, and mobilising opposition
They collect taxes from citizens
They appoint judges to courts
e: Losing parties play the role of Opposition, voicing alternative views and criticising government failures or wrong policies.

q: According to the Election Commission of India, what are the criteria for a party to be recognised as a "National Party"?
o: Securing 10% votes in just one state
Securing at least 6% of total valid votes in Lok Sabha elections or Assembly elections in four States and winning at least 4 seats in the Lok Sabha
Having at least 100 registered members
Winning at least 100 seats in Lok Sabha
e: A party that secures at least 6% of total votes in Lok Sabha elections or Assembly elections in four States and wins at least 4 seats in the Lok Sabha is recognised as a National Party.

q: What is the criterion laid down by the Election Commission for recognising a party as a "State Party"?
o: Securing at least 6% of total votes in an election to the Legislative Assembly of a State and winning at least 2 seats
Winning 10 seats across four states
Winning 20 seats in Lok Sabha
Winning 1 ward in a municipality
e: A party that secures at least 6% of the total votes in a State Legislative Assembly election and wins at least 2 seats is recognised as a State Party.

q: When several parties in a multi-party system join hands for contesting elections and winning power, what is it called?
o: Alliance or Front
One-party rule
Defection
President’s Rule
e: When multiple parties join hands to contest elections and win power, it is called an alliance or front (e.g., NDA, UPA, Left Front in India).

q: Parties such as Jharkhand Mukti Morcha (JMM), Samajwadi Party, or Rashtriya Janata Dal represent which broader category of parties?
o: State / Regional parties
Illegal outfits
Purely non-political pressure groups
International NGOs
e: Parties like JMM, RJD, Samajwadi Party, etc. are State/regional parties whose rise has strengthened federalism and coalition democracy in India.

q: What does the term "Partisan" mean?
o: Someone completely neutral and unconnected to any group
A person strongly committed to a party, group, or faction, marked by a tendency to take a side and inability to take a balanced view
An impartial Supreme Court judge
An Election Commission observer
e: A partisan is a person strongly committed to a party, group, or faction, showing a tendency to take a side rather than a balanced view.

q: In which year was the Communist Party of India (CPI) formed?
e: The Communist Party of India (CPI) was formed in 1925; later in 1964 it split leading to the formation of CPI(M).

q: From whose teachings and ideas does the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) draw inspiration?
o: Sahu Maharaj, Mahatma Phule, Periyar Ramaswami Naicker, and Babasaheb Ambedkar
Bismarck and Metternich
Lord Curzon and Clive
Napoleon Bonaparte
e: BSP seeks to secure power for the Bahujan Samaj (Dalits, Adivasis, OBCs, religious minorities) inspired by Sahu Maharaj, Mahatma Phule, Periyar, and Ambedkar.

q: What is meant by the first challenge faced by political parties: "lack of internal democracy"?
o: Concentration of power in one or a few top leaders, absence of proper membership registers, and failure to hold regular internal organisational elections
Registering the party with the Election Commission
Using EVMs in general elections
Holding Question Hour in Parliament
e: Parties often do not keep membership registers, do not hold organisational meetings, and fail to conduct regular internal elections, concentrating power at the top.

q: How does the challenge of "dynastic succession" affect political parties?
o: Top leaders give unfair advantage to family members or close associates, denying ordinary party workers a fair chance to rise to top positions
Only poor farmers become party chiefs
It strengthens internal transparency
It reduces election expenses to zero
e: Since most parties lack transparent functioning, top positions are often controlled by members of one family, which is unfair to other members and bad for democracy.

q: Why do voters often face a "lack of meaningful choice" among political parties today?
o: Because in recent years there has been a decline in ideological differences among parties in most parts of the world, offering similar fundamental policies
Because only one party contests elections
Because NOTA was removed
Because elections are held monthly
e: Declining ideological differences on major economic policies—and the same set of leaders shifting from one party to another—leave voters with few meaningful choices.

q: What measure was adopted through an amendment to the Indian Constitution to curb defection?
o: If any MLA or MP changes parties, he or she will lose their seat in the legislature
A defector is automatically appointed Minister
Defectors receive extra parliamentary funds
Opposition parties were banned
e: The Constitution was amended to prevent elected MLAs and MPs from changing parties; if any MLA or MP changes parties, they lose their seat in the legislature.

q: What is the suggested reform known as "State funding of elections"?
o: Government giving parties money or support (in kind like petrol, paper, telephone) to meet election expenses to curb the influence of big money
Charging citizens a voting tax at polling booths
Allowing unlimited secret corporate funding
Cancelling elections altogether
e: State funding of elections proposes that government gives parties money or resources based on votes secured in the previous election to curb money power.

q: Why does decision-making in a democracy take more time than in a non-democratic government?
o: Because democracy is based on the idea of deliberation, negotiation, and following proper norms and procedures
Because democratic leaders refuse to sign files
Because Parliament meets only once in five years
Because every decision requires a nationwide referendum
e: Democracy follows procedures of deliberation and negotiation; though it takes time, decisions are likely to be both more acceptable to people and more effective.

q: What did a survey across South Asian countries reveal about citizens’ support for democracy?
o: An overwhelming majority of people in South Asia support democracy and believe rule by elected representatives is suitable for their country
Most citizens prefer military dictatorship
No country in South Asia holds elections
Citizens overwhelmingly boycott democracy
e: Survey evidence from South Asia shows overwhelming support for democracy—people wish to be ruled by representatives elected by them.

q: On which front do democracies generally have a poor or disappointing record according to NCERT?
o: Often frustrating people’s needs, not always being free of corruption, and failing to significantly reduce economic inequalities
Refusing to hold regular elections
Denying citizens freedom of expression
Suppressing all opposition parties
e: Democracies often frustrate people’s needs, ignore demands of a majority of their population, are not free of corruption, and fail to sharply reduce economic inequality.

q: When comparing economic growth rates ONLY among "poor countries" (1950–2000), what is found between dictatorships and democracies?
o: The difference is virtually negligible (dictatorships ~4.34% vs democracies ~4.28%)
Democracies had 0% growth
Dictatorships achieved 20% growth
Poor democracies collapsed completely
e: Among poor countries, the gap in growth rates between dictatorships (4.34%) and democracies (4.28%) is negligible.

q: Besides the form of government, what other factors determine a country’s economic development?
o: Country’s population size, global situation, cooperation from other countries, and economic priorities adopted by the country
Only the national bird of the country
Height of the Parliament building
Number of sports stadiums
e: Economic development depends on several factors: country’s population size, global situation, cooperation from other countries, and economic priorities adopted.

q: What troubling trend regarding wealth distribution is observed within many democratic countries?
o: A small number of ultra-rich enjoy a highly disproportionate share of wealth and incomes while those at the bottom have very little to depend upon
The bottom 20% own 80% of national wealth
All salaries are equalised by law
Wealthy citizens have zero income
e: In democracies like South Africa and Brazil, the top 20% take over 60% of national income while the bottom 20% receive less than 3%.

q: Why can no regime permanently eliminate social differences, yet why is democracy best suited to handle them?
o: Because no society can fully and permanently resolve conflicts among different groups, but democracy teaches us to respect differences and negotiate peacefully
Because democracy bans minority languages
Because democracies have zero differences among citizens
Because military rule prevents all speech
e: No society can permanently eliminate conflicts among groups, but we can learn to respect these differences and evolve mechanisms to negotiate them—for which democracy is best suited.

q: Which two conditions MUST a democracy fulfil to successfully accommodate social diversity?
o: (1) The majority must always work with the minority, and (2) rule by majority must NOT become rule by the majority community in terms of religion, race, or language
(1) Majority community gets permanent monopoly, and (2) minorities cannot contest
(1) All parties are dissolved, and (2) one language is imposed
(1) Media censorship, and (2) emergency rule
e: A democracy must ensure: (1) majority always needs to work with minority so governments represent the general view, and (2) rule by majority must never turn into majority community dominance.

q: How has democracy strengthened the struggle for the dignity and equal treatment of women?
o: Once equality is accepted in principle in a democracy, it becomes easier for women to wage a struggle against what is now legally and morally unacceptable
Because women have stronger legal rights under dictatorships
Because democracy bans women from labour markets
Because courts refuse petitions by women
e: Long struggles by women created sensitivity that respect and equal treatment are necessary ingredients of a democratic society, giving women legal and moral ground to fight discrimination.

q: How has democracy in India helped disadvantaged and discriminated castes?
o: Democracy strengthened the claims of disadvantaged and discriminated castes for equal status and equal opportunity with legal and moral foundations
Democracy gave constitutional sanctity to caste hierarchy
Democracy abolished all social welfare schemes
Democracy removed voting rights of rural residents
e: Democracy in India has strengthened the claims of disadvantaged and discriminated castes for equal status and equal opportunity, removing legal/moral backing for caste atrocities.

q: What does the continuous complaint and criticism by citizens about democracy’s functioning actually demonstrate?
o: That democracy has failed and dictatorship is superior
That people have developed awareness and the ability to expect accountability and look critically at power-holders, transforming subjects into citizens
That citizens refuse to vote in elections
That the Election Commission has ceased operating
e: A public expression of dissatisfaction shows citizens have developed awareness and expect accountability—marking the transformation from the status of a subject into that of a citizen.

q: Which country does NCERT cite where over half of its population lives in poverty and people in several poor countries depend even for food supplies on rich countries?
o: Bangladesh
Switzerland
Japan
Germany
e: NCERT notes that in Bangladesh, more than half of its population lives in poverty, illustrating how democratically elected governments can struggle to eradicate poverty.

q: What conclusion does NCERT draw about the "cost of time" paid by democratic decision-making?
o: The cost of time that democracy pays is worth it because decisions following procedures are more likely to be effective and acceptable to the people
Democracy should be replaced by dictatorship to save time
No decision is ever implemented in a democracy
Elections should happen only once in 20 years
e: The cost of time that democracy pays is perhaps worth it because deliberated decisions are more likely to be acceptable to people and effective.

q: Which crucial warning about democratic outcomes does the example of Sri Lanka highlight?
o: That if majority rule turns into rule by the majority community refusing to share power with minorities, social harmony breaks down
That two-party systems always lead to civil war
That island countries cannot draft constitutions
That high GDP automatically eliminates ethnic conflict
e: Sri Lanka reminds us that a democracy must fulfil the conditions of power sharing and avoiding majority-community domination to sustain unity.

q: To measure whether a democracy provides an accountable government, what third institutional practice accompanies regular free/fair elections and open public debate?
o: Citizens’ right to information about the government and its functioning (transparency)
Imprisoning opposition party leaders
Allowing only state-controlled television
Keeping Parliament dissolved
e: Measuring an accountable democratic outcome focuses on regular free and fair elections, open public debate on major policies/legislations, and citizens’ right to information.

q: If there were no political parties and every candidate contested independently, how would it affect government formation and accountability?
o: No candidate could promise major policy changes; a government might form but its utility would remain uncertain and no one would be accountable for national governance
The country would instantly become the world’s largest economy
Every independent MP could enforce nationwide laws solo
Election expenses would vanish completely
e: Without parties, no candidate could make promises about major policy changes; elected representatives would be accountable only to their locality, with no one responsible for how the country is run.

q: Why has the rise of political parties become directly linked to the emergence of representative democracies?
o: Because large societies need an agency to gather different views on various issues, present them to government, bring representatives together, and form/restrain governments
Because large societies have no voters
Because courts select every MP
Because only wealthy citizens vote
e: Large representative democracies need agencies to aggregate diverse views, bring representatives together for responsible governance, make policies, and oppose/support government.

q: Which party system—one-party, two-party, or multi-party—is universally ideal according to NCERT?
o: No single system is ideal for all countries; party systems evolve over a long time depending on the nature of society, social/regional divisions, history of politics, and electoral system
One-party system is ideal for all nations
Only two-party systems are truly democratic
India must immediately enforce a two-party law
e: No party system is ideal for all countries; it is not something any country can choose freely, as it evolves based on social diversity, regional divisions, and election systems.

q: Why has India evolved a multi-party system while the USA largely has a two-party system?
o: Because social and geographical diversity in such a large country as India is not easily absorbed by two or even three parties
Because the US Constitution bans third parties by law
Because India has only indirect voting
Because the US has no states
e: India has evolved a multi-party system because the social and geographical diversity in such a large country is not easily absorbed by two or even three parties.

q:
Match the political parties with their founding year and symbol:
A. Indian National Congress (INC)
B. Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)
C. Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP)
D. National People’s Party (NPP)
o: A-1885 (Hand), B-1980 (Lotus), C-1984 (Elephant), D-2013 (Book)
A-1980 (Hand), B-1885 (Lotus), C-1984 (Book), D-2013 (Elephant)
A-1885 (Lotus), B-1984 (Hand), C-1925 (Elephant), D-2012 (Broom)
A-1964 (Sickle), B-1980 (Lotus), C-1999 (Clock), D-2013 (Book)
e: INC (1885, Hand), BJP (1980, Lotus), BSP (1984, Elephant), and NPP (2013, Book) match accurately.

q: Suppose a political party secures 8% valid votes and wins 3 seats each in Assembly elections of two states, and holds 1 seat in Lok Sabha. How will it be classified under ECI rules?
o: Recognised as a State Party (not a National Party, since National Party requires 4 states/LS 6% votes and 4 LS seats)
Recognised as a National Party immediately
Declared an illegal outfit
Registered only as a Municipal association
e: National Party recognition requires 6% votes in Lok Sabha or 4 State Assemblies plus at least 4 Lok Sabha seats; hence it qualifies as a State Party (6% votes + 2 Assembly seats).

q: Which reform order did the Election Commission of India pass to promote accountability inside political parties?
o: Made it necessary for political parties to hold their organisational elections and file their income tax returns
Banned all regional parties
Cancelled candidate affidavits
Enacted mandatory state funding of elections
e: The Election Commission passed an order making it necessary for political parties to hold their organisational elections and file their income tax returns.

q: What has been a mixed or unintended side-effect of the Anti-Defection constitutional amendment?
o: While it helped bring down defection, it has also made dissent more difficult inside parties as MPs/MLAs have to accept whatever party leaders decide
It ended parliamentary elections in India
No coalition government could form afterwards
It abolished secret ballot
e: The law brought defection down, yet made any dissent even more difficult because MPs and MLAs must obey whatever top party leaders decide.

q: Identify the accurate set of FOUR major challenges facing political parties worldwide and in India:
o: Lack of internal democracy, dynastic succession, growing role of money and muscle power, and lack of meaningful choice to voters
Excessive internal elections, total absence of funds, single national language, compulsory voting
Absence of Election Commission, voting age 35, lack of Supreme Court
Women reservation, coalition alliances, free press
e: The four key challenges to political parties are lack of internal democracy, dynastic succession, growing role of money and muscle power, and lack of meaningful choice.

q: Why must citizens be cautious about over-regulating political parties through rigid laws alone?
o: Because parties always find ways to cheat overly strict laws, and political leaders will not pass laws they themselves strongly dislike
Because Parliament lacks legislative authority
Because courts ban all parliamentary statutes
Because parties do not contest state elections
e: Over-regulation can be counter-productive as parties find ways to bypass laws; public pressure and citizen participation in parties are crucial complements.

q: Besides legal orders, in what TWO ways can ordinary citizens push political parties to reform?
o: (1) Putting public pressure through petitions, publicity, and agitations, and (2) citizens joining political parties themselves to improve politics from within
(1) Boycotting all elections permanently, and (2) abolishing democracy
(1) Stopping tax payments, and (2) closing courts
(1) Banning local bodies, and (2) censoring newspapers
e: Citizens can reform parties through public pressure (petitions, media, agitations) and by joining political parties themselves—replacing bad politics with better politics.

q: How do political parties provide people access to government machinery and welfare schemes?
o: An ordinary citizen finds it easier to approach a local party leader than a government officer, forcing parties to be responsive to people’s needs
Parties print currency for citizens
Parties replace all district courts
Parties grant visas directly
e: For an ordinary citizen it is easy to approach a local party leader than a government officer; hence people feel close to parties even when they do not fully trust them.

q: What has been the impact of the expansion in the number and strength of State (regional) parties in India over the last three decades?
o: It made Parliament politically more diverse and compelled national parties to form alliances with State parties, strengthening federalism and democracy
It turned India into a unitary state
It abolished Lok Sabha elections
It eliminated State Legislative Assemblies
e: Since 1996, nearly every major State party has got an opportunity to be part of national coalition governments, strengthening federalism and democracy in India.

q: What mandatory measure did the Supreme Court introduce to reduce the influence of money and criminals in elections?
o: Made it mandatory for every candidate contesting elections to file an Affidavit giving details of property and pending criminal cases
Banned all wealthy individuals from politics permanently
Imposed 100% tax on party membership
Replaced ballot boxes with smartphones
e: The Supreme Court ordered every candidate to file an Affidavit disclosing assets and criminal cases, providing public information—though checking accuracy remains a gap.

q: The reform proposal requiring political parties to give about one-third of tickets to women and reserve a quota in party decision-making bodies addresses what issue?
o: Chronic under-representation of women in elections, legislatures, and party leadership
Solely the problem of legislative defection
International trade deficits
Duplication of party symbols
e: Making it mandatory for political parties to give at least one-third of tickets to women and setting a quota in party decision-making bodies directly targets low female representation.

q: Why might a non-democratic government take fast decisions that nevertheless face problems in practice?
o: Because decisions taken swiftly without deliberation or public consultation may not be accepted by the people and may face severe resistance
Because dictatorships never collect taxes
Because democracies have no ministries
Because dictatorships rule only villages
e: A non-democratic regime can take fast decisions, yet those decisions may not be accepted by people and run into problems; democratic deliberation builds legitimacy and effectiveness.

q: Evaluating the actual record of democracies on corruption and responsiveness, which statement is most accurate?
o: Democracies are not free of corruption and often frustrate people’s needs, yet there is nothing to show non-democracies are less corrupt or more sensitive
Dictatorships have zero corruption anywhere in the world
Corruption is legally encouraged in democracies
Every democracy is 100% corruption-free
e: While democracies have a dismal record in curbing corruption or always being attentive, non-democracies are neither less corrupt nor more sensitive to people’s needs.

q: Based on economic growth comparisons (1950–2000), what practical conclusion does NCERT draw about choosing between democracy and dictatorship?
o: Democracy is not a guarantee of rapid economic development, but we can expect it not to lag behind dictatorships, making democracy preferable for its many broader outcomes
Countries should adopt dictatorship purely for GDP growth
Dictatorship guarantees wealth for every poor citizen
Economic growth is impossible under democracy
e: Even though democracy does not guarantee higher growth, the gap among poor nations is negligible and democracy offers vastly superior political and human outcomes.

q: What contradiction is highlighted in the statement: "Democracies are based on political equality, yet we find growing economic inequalities"?
o: All citizens carry equal weight in electing representatives, yet a small ultra-rich minority controls a disproportionate share of income and wealth while the bottom struggles for basic needs
Rich citizens legally get two votes each
Only poor citizens sit in Parliament
Savings banks are banned in democracies

Country X will collapse immediately

That elections should cease once development finishes

q: What is the most balanced evaluation of whether democratic governments are "efficient"?

Partisanship

o: Both are relatively new parties formed during 2012–2013 that expanded across states to earn National Party recognition
Both were founded in 1885
Both share the Lotus symbol
Both restrict themselves to one municipality
e: Formed in 2012 and 2013 respectively, both AAP and NPP expanded across multiple states to qualify for National Party status.

q:
Read these three statements regarding the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP):
1. It traces its roots to the Bharatiya Jana Sangh formed by Syama Prasad Mukherjee in 1951.
2. It emphasises cultural nationalism (Hindutva), full integration of Jammu & Kashmir, and a Uniform Civil Code.
3. Founded in 1980, it came to power at the Centre in 1998 as leader of the NDA.
Which are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
All 1, 2 and 3
e: All three statements accurately reflect the BJP’s historical origin, ideological pillars, and rise as summarised in NCERT.

q: If the Opposition becomes extremely weak or is silenced in a democracy, what is the biggest danger?
o: The ruling party faces little check on policy errors or misuse of power, depriving citizens of an organised platform to voice dissent and alternatives
All election expenses vanish
Laws automatically become fairer without debate
Every citizen becomes a cabinet minister
e: Opposition keeps governments accountable by exposing flaws and mobilising dissent; without a strong opposition, power risks becoming unchecked.

q:
Consider the following statements about democracy:
1. Democracy can only create conditions for achieving goals; citizens have to take advantage of those conditions.
2. While democracies hold regular elections, their actual record on sharing complete information and subjecting every decision to public debate is mixed.
3. Despite slowness or inefficiencies, democracy’s chief political advantage is being people’s own legitimate government.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
All 1, 2 and 3
e: All three statements accurately capture the realistic expectations, mixed empirical track record, and foundational legitimacy of democracy.

q: Which statement does NOT align with (is FALSE about) the 1950–2000 economic data comparing regimes in NCERT?
o: Overall, average growth rate of democracies (3.95%) was slightly lower than dictatorships (4.42%)
Among poor countries, dictatorships (4.34%) and democracies (4.28%) had nearly identical growth rates
In several unequal democracies, the top 20% take over 50–65% of national income
Every democratic nation guarantees the world’s fastest GDP growth rate and complete economic equality
e: Democracy guarantees neither the fastest economic growth nor automatic economic equality.

q: If a majority religious or linguistic group permanently monopolises power and refuses to work with minorities, which conditions for accommodating social diversity are violated?
o: Violation of BOTH conditions: majority must work with minority, and rule by majority must never become rule by the majority community
Violation only of the GDP growth condition
Violation only of one-party system rules
Violation only of RTI deadlines
e: Both core conditions are violated—majority must work with minority, and majority must not turn into domination by a majority religious/racial/linguistic community.

q: Dictatorship X reports 6% growth with strict press censorship and suppression of minorities. Democracy Y sees 5.5% growth, open media debate exposing scandals, and regular elections that can vote out leaders. What is the correct democratic evaluation?
o: Country Y is far superior because negligible growth differences cannot outweigh transparency, free media accountability, minority protection, and legitimate citizen power
Country X is superior because citizens should trade freedom for 0.5% extra GDP
Both countries are equally authoritarian
Country Y should ban independent media
e: Negligible economic growth differences never justify surrendering transparency, civil liberties, minority accommodation, and the right to replace rulers.

q: Why does NCERT say that public complaints against democracy are actually a testimony to its success?
o: Because complaints prove citizens have developed awareness, critically evaluate power-holders, and believe their vote matters—transforming passive subjects into active citizens
Because complaining in a democracy leads to jail
Because dictatorships encourage public protests
Because democracy delivers zero outcomes
e: When people get some benefits of democracy, they ask for more; critical expectations show people have become active citizens rather than silent subjects.

q: What is the direct link between the "challenges to political parties" and the "outcomes of democracy"?
o: Only when parties become internally democratic, transparent, and clean from money/muscle power can democratic governments deliver more responsive, clean, and equitable outcomes
There is zero link between political parties and democratic outcomes
Less internal democracy inside parties automatically creates transparency
Dynastic politics eliminates poverty
e: Political parties run democratic governments; hence reforming parties directly improves accountability, reduces corruption, and strengthens democratic outcomes.

q: Which scenario accurately illustrates the true democratic meaning of "rule by majority"?
o: On an environmental bill Parties A and C form a majority, whereas on an education bill Parties A, B, and independents form a majority—allowing shifting majorities by issue
An 80% religious community permanently bars the remaining 20% from contesting elections
One royal family holds the PM post forever
All losing opposition MPs are jailed after results
e: True democratic majority rule means different persons and groups can form majorities on different issues and elections, rather than permanent domination by birth.

q: What realistic assessment does NCERT give about "dignity and equal treatment of women" in democracies?
o: We cannot claim women are always treated with respect everywhere, yet long struggles created sensitivity and legal-moral recognition that makes fighting discrimination far easier in democracies
Gender discrimination vanished 100% the day democracy began
Non-democratic regimes give stronger legal remedies to women
Women never had to struggle for rights in democracies
e: Historically most societies were male-dominated, yet in democracy women’s equality gained legal and moral recognition, empowering continued struggles against injustice.

q: Which statement best captures BOTH the achievement and remaining challenge of Indian democracy regarding caste inequalities?
o: Achievement: Strengthened claims of disadvantaged castes for equal status and opportunity; Challenge: Caste inequalities and atrocities still exist in practice, though lacking legal or moral foundation
Achievement: Caste completely vanished from India; Challenge: None left
Achievement: Upper castes got double votes; Challenge: Lower castes cannot contest
Achievement: Zero progress; Challenge: Democracy created caste hierarchy
e: Democracy gave disadvantaged castes moral and legal backing for equal status and opportunity; though inequalities and atrocities persist, they no longer have legal or moral sanction.

q: A political party appeals exclusively to one communal vote bank while cancelling all internal organisational elections. Which two distinct democratic problems are present here?
o: Communal political mobilisation AND lack of internal democracy within the party
Economic liberalisation AND Right to Information
Federalism AND two-party system
Feminism AND occupational mobility
e: Polarising along religious lines reflects communal mobilisation, while skipping organisational elections indicates lack of internal democracy.

q: Why are citizens in many democracies dissatisfied with their governments’ performance even while strongly supporting democracy as an idea?
o: Because actual democratic governments often fall short on curbing corruption, reducing economic inequalities, and promptly addressing needs of the majority population
Because citizens secretly prefer military coups
Because free elections happen too frequently
Because citizens oppose transparency laws
e: Citizens cherish democracy in principle yet critique flawed governments for corruption, slow responsiveness, and persistent economic inequality—demanding better democracy, not dictatorship.

q:
Which pair correctly matches the core ideological focus of two major Indian National Parties in NCERT?
1. Welfare and power for "Bahujan Samaj" inspired by Sahu Maharaj, Phule, Periyar, and Ambedkar
2. Cultural nationalism (Hindutva) and "Integral Humanism / Antyodaya"
o: 1 — Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP); 2 — Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)
1 — BJP; 2 — BSP
1 — INC; 2 — CPI(M)
1 — CPI; 2 — NPP
e: BSP represents the Bahujan Samaj inspired by Sahu Maharaj, Phule, Periyar, and Ambedkar; BJP centres on cultural nationalism and Integral Humanism/Antyodaya.

q: Identify the FALSE statement regarding transparency and accountability in democratic governments:
o: In a democracy citizens have the right to choose their rulers and exercise control over them
Citizens have the right to examine whether decisions were taken through proper norms and procedures
Every democratic government works exclusively in total secrecy and never holds regular elections
Laws like RTI give citizens effective means to monitor governance
e: Working in total secrecy without regular elections characterises dictatorship, not democracy.

q: What broad constitutional/ideological principle do INC, CPI(M), and NCP share in their stated programme as summarised in NCERT?
o: Commitment to Secularism and Democracy
Establishing one-party dictatorship
Abolishing universal adult suffrage
Replacing federalism with monarchy
e: Across their NCERT party profiles, INC, CPI(M), and NCP all profess commitment to secularism and democracy alongside their distinct economic/political emphases.

q: What is the combined practical takeaway from studying "Political Parties" and "Outcomes of Democracy"?
o: Democratic success is never automatic; achieving accountable, just, and inclusive outcomes requires reforming political parties and active participation by aware, questioning citizens
After voting once, citizens should completely withdraw from public affairs for five years
Dictatorship is the most reliable path to equality
Replacing multi-party competition with one party solves all challenges
e: Democracy only creates enabling conditions; reforming political parties and active, vigilant citizenship are what turn democratic ideals into real-world outcomes.
